o: Shift an unsigned eight-bit binary number left or right.
Explain the relationship between shifts and powers of two.

Convert 00110101₂ to denary.
Add 00001111 and 00000001 in binary.
An eight-bit number is 11010110₂. Express it in hexadecimal and then denary.
c: A shift moves bit positions
Move every bit the same number of columns. Keep the length at eight bits.
Left shift
Move every bit left and add zeros at the right. For an unsigned value, shifting by n places multiplies by 2ⁿ only when no 1 is shifted off the eight-bit end.
Right shift
Move every bit right and insert zeros at the left. For an unsigned value, n places means divide by 2ⁿ, discarding any remainder and bits shifted off the edge.
Bits can be lost
The revision guide's ×2 / ÷2 memory aid is a shortcut, not a substitute for shifting the actual bits. Always show the eight-bit result: any 1 that moves beyond the edge is lost.

m.q: Shift 00010110 left by 2 places. Explain each step.
st: Label the eight bit positions 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Start with 00010110, which is 16 + 4 + 2 = 22.
Move every bit two positions to the left; fill two positions on the right with zeros.
The eight-bit result is 01011000, which is 88.
Check: 22 × 2² = 88. This time no 1 was lost.

w: Shift 00101000 right by one place.
00010100, representing 20 rather than 40.
Shift 00001101 left by two places.
00110100, representing 52.
Why does 11000000 shifted left by two places not show 768?
The two leading 1s leave the eight-bit register, so the result is 00000000.

k.q: Predict the displayed answer and complete a one-line change on your MWB.
p: Predict the output of this program.
Change the arithmetic to model a two-place left shift.
Explain when multiplying by a power of two is NOT the same as an 8-bit shift.
k.a: 24; for two places write print(value * 4), giving 48. If bits are discarded by the eight-bit limit the arithmetic model can differ. On this lesson, pupils begin on MWBs; the teacher may then introduce running code in the OCR ERL editor.

e: Perform an 8-bit logical right shift of 10110000 by three places. [2]
00010110. All bits move three places right and zeroes fill from the left.
Describe the effect of shifting the unsigned number 00001101 left by TWO places, including its denary value. [3]
00001101 is 13 [1]; moving two places left gives 00110100 [1], which is 52 = 13 × 2² [1].
A pupil claims shifting 10000000 left once gives 256 in an 8-bit register. Explain the mistake. [2]
The 1 is shifted out and lost; the eight-bit result is 00000000, not 256.
v: Moving each bit left or right, filling empty positions with zero.
The leftmost bit with the highest place value.
The rightmost bit with the smallest place value.
A result that cannot fit into the available number of bits.
x: A one-place logical right shift always adds a zero on the left.

Use sequential ASCII codes and calculate character-set capacity.
r: Perform a one-place logical left shift on 00101100.
Convert hexadecimal 7B to denary.
Perform a two-place logical right shift on 10110001. Explain what happens to the bits that leave the right-hand side.
00101100. The two bits shifted beyond the right edge are discarded.
c: Character sets
Each character is mapped to a numerical code stored in binary. The same bit pattern has meaning only when the encoding or character set is known.
ASCII · numbers in sequence

Standard ASCII has 128 codes, numbered 0–127 (7 bits). Codes are often shown as eight-bit bytes with a leading zero. A=65 (01000001), B=66 (01000010), C=67 (01000011). Adjacent capital letters have consecutive codes.
Unicode · more scripts and symbols

Unicode supports far more characters than standard ASCII, including multiple languages, symbols and emojis. The number of bytes per character depends on the encoding, so do not assume all Unicode text always uses 16 or 32 bits.
Apply the booklet method
Given the ASCII code for one capital letter, move forward or back one code at a time; preserve the correct eight-bit width when asked. Also remember: n bits can represent 2ⁿ different values.

m.q: Given the ASCII byte for B = 01000010, explain how to find the code for C.
st: The eight displayed bits include a leading zero: standard ASCII uses seven-bit codes.
Capital letters are assigned consecutive ASCII values.
B is denary 66, so C is the next code, denary 67.
Write 67 in eight-bit form: 01000011. This is C.
A character set maps the code to a particular character; the binary itself does not spell the letter.

w: Given capital H is 01001000 in ASCII, write the eight-bit code for I.
I is the next capital letter, so add 1: 01001001.
A character set has 6 bits per character. How many codes?
Why might Unicode be preferable for a multilingual school?
It can represent many more scripts and special symbols than standard ASCII.

k.q: Complete the character-code program on your mini-whiteboard.
p: Write one instruction to display the word 'Hello' rather than its numerical code.
k.a: Initially displays 65; change to characterCode = 66; a valid third line is print("Hello"). The numeric code is not automatically converted to its character by print().

e:
The eight-bit ASCII code for C is 01000011. Work out the ASCII codes for D, E and F. [3]

A standard character set with 128 codes, represented by seven bits; often stored in eight-bit bytes.
Character encoding standard that supports a much wider range of scripts and symbols.

o: Describe a bitmap as a grid of pixels.
Explain resolution, colour depth and metadata.
Predict the effects of changing image settings.
r: What is a character set?
A collection of characters, each assigned a numerical/binary code.
Convert hexadecimal 2F to denary.
Standard ASCII uses seven bits. Calculate the number of possible codes and explain why Unicode is useful.
2⁷ = 128 codes. Unicode supports a much wider range of characters, writing systems and symbols.
c: Bitmap images
Like the coloured square grids in the revision booklet, a bitmap is made from pixels. Each pixel is stored using a binary colour code.
Resolution
Width × height in pixels. More pixels normally produce more detail and larger uncompressed files.
Colour depth
Colour depth is bits per pixel: one bit allows 2 colours; two bits allow 4; three bits allow 8; and four bits allow 16. Do not confuse bit depth with the number of pixels.
Metadata
Metadata describes the image rather than its picture content. Examples include width, height and colour depth; such information can help software or search services identify files.

m.q: Work out the colour possibilities of a small bitmap.
st: Draw a 4 × 3 grid. It contains 12 pixels.
Suppose each pixel uses 2 bits.
List possible binary codes: 00, 01, 10 and 11.
Therefore each pixel can be one of four coded colours.
Total raw pixel data: 12 × 2 = 24 bits (metadata excluded).

w: How many pixels are in a 6 × 4 bitmap?
6 × 4 = 24 pixels.
An 8 × 8 bitmap uses 2-bit colour depth. How many colours can each pixel represent?
2² = 4 possible colour codes for each pixel. The image's 64 pixels do not change the number of colours available per pixel.
Explain why 8-bit colour depth uses more storage than 4-bit at the same resolution.
Each pixel requires twice as many bits (8 rather than 4).

k.a: 12 pixels; changing width to 6 gives 18; print(width * height * 2) gives the pixel data in bits (36 with the revised width).

e: A bitmap is 10 pixels wide and 8 high. Calculate the pixel count. [2]

State what colour depth measures, then calculate the maximum colours at 5 bits per pixel. [3]
Bits used for each pixel; 2⁵ = 32 colours.
An image has metadata listing its width as 800 pixels and height as 600 pixels. Explain what metadata is and give ONE use of this information. [3]
Metadata is data about a file rather than the image pixels [1]. Here it records width and height [1], which software can use to display or organise the image correctly [1].
v: Smallest individual coloured element in a bitmap.
Width and height measured in pixels.
Number of bits used for each pixel.
Data about the image, such as dimensions and colour depth.
x: A bitmap with higher colour depth can represent more colours per pixel.

o: Calculate an uncompressed bitmap’s raw pixel-data size.
Convert image sizes from bits to bytes.
Explain the impact of resolution and colour depth.
r: A bitmap is six pixels wide and four pixels high. How many pixels does it contain?
6 × 4 = 24 pixels.
Convert hexadecimal 9A to denary.
How many different codes can seven bits represent?
A bitmap is 10 × 8 pixels with three-bit colour depth. Calculate its total number of pixels and the maximum number of colours per pixel.
80 pixels; 2³ = 8 possible colours.
c: Booklet method: count the pixels
Width × height = number of pixels. Always label the units as pixels before applying colour depth.
Multiply by colour depth
Raw pixel data (bits) = width × height × colour depth (bits per pixel). This is the same formula used in the Paper 1 revision booklet.
Convert into bytes and MB
Divide the bit count by 8 for bytes. For decimal units as used in the booklet: ÷1000 for KB, then ÷1000 for MB. Follow the unit definition in an exam question.
Be precise about size
The calculation gives uncompressed pixel data only. Headers, metadata and compression can change the actual size of a saved file.
Show the full calculation
Use five steps: pixels → bits → bytes → KB → MB when MB are requested. Keep units on every line.

m.q: Calculate the raw size of a 200 × 100 image at 8-bit colour.
st: Identify width = 200 and height = 100 pixels.
Multiply by colour depth: 20,000 × 8 = 160,000 bits.
Divide by 8: 160,000 ÷ 8 = 20,000 bytes.
For the decimal units used in the guide, 20,000 bytes = 20 KB. Metadata and compression are excluded.

w: Find bits for a 40 × 20 image at 4 bits per pixel.
Convert 3,200 bits to bytes.
An image’s colour depth rises from 4 to 8. How does raw size change?
It doubles at the same width and height.

p: Predict the number of bits displayed.

o: Explain how analogue sound is represented digitally.
Distinguish sample rate from bit depth.
Explain effects on quality and uncompressed file size.
r: Calculate the raw size of a 20 × 10 bitmap with four-bit colour depth. Give bits and bytes.
Perform a two-place logical right shift on 00110000.
State one advantage of Unicode over standard ASCII.
Unicode represents a much wider range of characters and writing systems.
An uncompressed bitmap is 64 × 32 pixels at four bits per pixel. Calculate its raw pixel-data size in bytes.
c: Analogue sound is continuous
Sound is a changing wave. The microphone's electrical signal represents that wave; a digital file stores measurements instead of storing the continuous signal directly.
Sampling · regular snapshots
Imagine taking equally spaced snapshots of the wave's height (amplitude). Each sample records an amplitude at one point in time.
Sample rate · how often
Sample rate is how many snapshots are taken in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). More samples per second can capture more detail but use more storage.
Bit depth · how precisely
Bit depth is how many bits represent each measured amplitude. Greater bit depth allows more possible levels for each sample, not more samples per second.
Connect to file size
For raw uncompressed mono sound: sample rate × duration × bit depth = number of bits. This formula is modelled in the next lesson.

m.q: Sketch how a continuous sound becomes digital samples.
st: Draw a smooth analogue wave on a time axis.
Place five equally spaced vertical sample positions: these are regular snapshots of the wave, matching the revision booklet diagram.
At each position, mark the wave’s amplitude.
Turn each measured amplitude into a binary value.

w: At 1,000 Hz, how many samples are taken each second?
1,000 samples.
At 4,000 samples/s for 3 s, how many samples?

Explain the difference between sample rate and bit depth.
Sample rate is measurements per second; bit depth is bits stored per measurement.

k.q: Start by modelling a sample count in OCR ERL.

k.a: 6,000 samples initially; 10,000 samples at 5 s; bitDepth = 8 and print(rate * seconds * bitDepth) gives 80,000 bits for the revised duration.

e: Describe sound sampling. [2]
Measure the amplitude of an analogue signal at regular intervals and represent each sample digitally.
State the unit of sample rate. [1]
Hertz (Hz), samples per second.
Explain how increasing sample rate and increasing bit depth affect the quality and uncompressed size of a sound file. [4]

Higher sample rate provides more measurements per second [1], which can improve representation and increases file size [1]. Higher bit depth offers more distinct amplitude levels [1], which can improve representation and increases bits per sample/file size [1].
v: Measuring an analogue signal’s amplitude at intervals.
Number of amplitude measurements per second.
Bits used to represent each sound sample.
x: Bit depth means how many samples are taken each second.
